narratives.narrative: Here the godly (chasid) is read not as a present quality but as an absence grieved: sense (101) = 'the godly have vanished'. Its type (102) is affect, not status — the item registers in the interior as felt grief. There is no source (103 present:false): the psalmist does not name what produced the loss, so the reading rests on the fact of it, not its cause. Seat (104) = none — the grief is not organ-located; it is a whole-self lament, not a movement of a named faculty. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, and the operation (106) is his lament that the godly one is gone and the faithful have disappeared from among men — grief at the collapse of faithfulness itself. Target (107) is lament-over-loss: the movement turns not outward against enemies but inward-and-back upon a vanished good. Manner (108) is none, and intensity, specifier and effect are all absent (109-111 present:false) — the psalm states the loss flatly, without measuring its degree, qualifying it, or naming a downstream result; the silence says the fact alone is the weight. Coupling (112) = godly-vanished, binding the item to its own disappearance — the characteristic is coupled to its own negation. No prohibition (113 present:false) is in view. Discovery (114): the interior grieves a social collapse — it can no longer find a trustworthy person. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = internal:ib-state — this is an inner condition, the felt state of a self that scans its world and finds no one faithful. Directive 5 requires reading descent as fully as ascent: this is the faith-family in its failure mode, faithfulness experienced as loss.
narratives.story: The psalmist looks around for someone he can trust and finds no one. He cries out that the good and faithful people have simply disappeared from among ordinary men. This is not a calm observation but raw grief — an ache spread through his whole being rather than a single passing feeling. He does not explain how it came to this or blame a particular cause; he just states the bare, heavy fact and lets it stand. There is no measuring of how bad it is and no talk of what will come next — the loss itself is the whole weight. What the passage shows is a person whose inner world has been emptied of trustworthy company, and who feels that emptiness as a wound.
narratives.variation_note: Of the three 'godly' readings, this one alone reads the characteristic as ABSENCE and as affect (grief), not status: the godly are gone, and the item lives in the interior as lament (locus internal:ib-state, bearer the psalmist). It is the descent pole of the item, against Psa 52:9 (the godly as an external company he waits among) and Psa 86:2 (the godly as the psalmist's own claimed devotion).

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = 'I believe I shall see his goodness'; the item is belief as a forward-leaning conviction about what the future holds. Type (102) is affect — here believing is not a bare cognitive assent but a felt steadying of the self. No source (103 present:false) is named: the psalm does not derive the belief from a prior cause but presents it as the interior's own act. Seat (104) = none — belief is not lodged in a named organ; it is the whole self's posture. Bearer (105) is the psalmist; operation (106) = the self believes it will look upon the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living, a faith that steadies against despair. Target (107) = sustaining-faith: the movement's endpoint is the holding-up of the self. Manner (108) is none; intensity, specifier and effect are all absent (109-111 present:false) — the text does not grade the belief's strength, qualify it, or trace a result beyond the steadying itself. Coupling (112) = believe-to-see: belief is bound to a coming sight, faith reaching toward future vision. No prohibition (113). Discovery (114): the operation is the faith that keeps the interior from collapse — belief that it will yet see good is what holds it, framed against the false witnesses and violence of v12. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = internal:ib-state — an inner condition that props the self up under threat. God is the arena toward which the belief looks; the inner-being process is the self holding itself steady by expecting good.
narratives.story: Hemmed in by enemies and lying witnesses, the psalmist makes a quiet, load-bearing declaration: he believes he will still see good things from the Lord while he is alive. This is more than an idea in his head — it is a feeling that props him up and keeps him from caving in to despair. He does not argue for it or say where the confidence came from; it is simply the stance his heart takes. And he does not measure how strong it is or spell out what it will lead to — the point is that this expectation of coming good is exactly what holds him together. His believing reaches forward toward a day when he will see the Lord's goodness, and that forward reach is what keeps his inner self from collapsing.
narratives.variation_note: Among the six 'believe' readings this is the only one typed as affect and read as ascent from the psalmist's own mouth: belief as a felt anchor against despair (target sustaining-faith, coupling believe-to-see). It contrasts with the disposition-typed failures of Psa 78:22/78:32/106:24 and the held-belief of Psa 116:10 and 119:66.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = truth (emeth) as 'the cause of truth' — truth here is not a private inner honesty but a public moral cause the king rides out to establish. Type (102) is status: truth names a standing condition, a value the king embodies and advances, not an event that happens. No source (103 present:false): the psalm does not trace where this truth arises; it is simply the cause he champions. Seat (104) = none — truth is not located in a named organ; it is a value carried, not an organ-movement. Bearer (105) is the king (his cause). Operation (106) = none and target (107) = none: strikingly, this truth performs no interior operation and reaches no interior target — the silence is evidence that here emeth functions as a standing banner, not a working movement within a self; it is what the king rides FOR, not something his inner being does. Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier and effect are absent (109-111 present:false) — no degree, qualifier, or result is recorded, consistent with truth-as-status rather than truth-as-act. Coupling (112) is a pair: truth is bound with meekness and righteousness — the first of a triad of virtues the king advances together. No prohibition (113). Discovery (114): 'ride out victoriously for the cause of truth and meekness and righteousness' — emeth is the moral cause the king's rule advances. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = internal:ib-state — though its bearer is the royal cause, the item is still filed as an inner-being condition: truth as a value seated in the person of the king. The inner-being reading is thin here by design (directive 7): truth appears as a championed standing, with its operation and target explicitly empty.
narratives.story: In this royal wedding song the king is pictured riding out in majesty to fight for a cause, and the first thing named in that cause is truth — set alongside gentleness and doing right. Truth here is not a hidden honesty tucked inside a person; it is a public banner, a standing value the king openly champions and works to establish in his realm. The song does not say where this truth comes from or picture it stirring anything inside him; it simply names it as the thing he stands for. It is bound together with meekness and righteousness, three virtues advanced as one. So truth appears less as something moving within a heart and more as a worthy cause a good ruler carries — a value he embodies rather than a feeling he experiences.
narratives.variation_note: The two 'truth' readings split outward vs inward. Here truth is a PUBLIC moral cause borne by the king (bearer = the king's cause; operation and target both 'none'; paired with meekness and righteousness) — truth as championed standing. Psa 51:6 reads the same emeth as INNER truthfulness in the inward being (seat present, bearer the penitent, locus internal:heart). The shift in bearer and seat is the finding: the same word names both a public cause and the honesty of the hidden self.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = the godly / faithful ones (chasidim). Type (102) is status — a standing identity, the covenant-loyal, not an act. Uniquely in this family, source (103) is present: the faithful ones are summoned by God who comes to judge (v1,3-4) — a pair binding their gathering to God's advent. This is evidence: their standing is defined by being called, by the summons rather than by an inner initiative of their own. Seat (104) = none — no organ locates the identity; it is a whole-person belonging. Bearer (105) = the faithful / godly ones (chasidim). Operation (106) = none and target (107) = none: the reading records no interior movement and no interior target — the silence says these faithful ones are, at this moment, objects of a summons, not agents performing an operation; their inner-being contribution is their standing readiness to be gathered, not an act. Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier, effect absent (109-111 present:false). Coupling (112) = none — no other item is welded to this one here; the faithful ones stand alone before the Judge. No prohibition (113). Discovery (114): 'Gather to me my faithful ones, who made a covenant with me by sacrifice' — the covenant-loyal summoned before the Judge, the true worshippers distinguished from the wicked (v16). Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = external:god — the item's frame of reference is God who gathers, the arena toward which their loyalty is defined. The inner-being process is a standing loyalty that answers a summons: identity constituted by covenant and call rather than by any recorded interior act.
narratives.story: As God arrives to judge, wrapped in fire and storm, he issues a command: gather my faithful ones to me — the people who bound themselves to him by covenant and sacrifice. What defines these faithful ones here is not something they are actively doing but the fact that they are being called; their identity is set by God's summons. The passage does not show them stirring with any particular feeling or reaching for anything; they simply stand as those who belong to God and are ready to be gathered. Nothing else is tied to them in the moment — they stand alone before their Judge. Their faithfulness is a steady loyalty, rooted in covenant, that answers when God calls, and it marks them off from the wicked he will later confront.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = truth / faithfulness (emeth) 'in the inward being' — here emeth is inner truthfulness, the honesty of the hidden self, not an outward cause. Type (102) is status: a standing condition God desires within. Source (103) is present as a pair: truth is what God delights in / desires (v6) — its origin-frame is the divine delight that seeks it. Seat (104) is present, and this is the family's one located reading: 'in the inward being' — a pair binding truth to the deep interior (tuchoth), the hidden self. That the seat is named here (against 'none' everywhere else) is itself the finding: this is truth precisely as an interior organ-condition. Bearer (105) = the penitent. Operation (106) = none and target (107) = none — no discrete interior act or object is recorded; truth is a state God wants IN the self, not an operation the self performs. Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier, effect absent (109-111 present:false) — no degree or result is graded; the point is the presence or absence of the condition itself. Coupling (112) is a pair: truth is bound with wisdom taught in the secret heart — the interior honesty God desires is answered by wisdom imparted in the hidden place. No prohibition (113). Discovery (114): the integrity God desires deep within; inner truthfulness, not outward conformity — the honesty of the hidden self, what God's delight seeks, answered by wisdom taught in the secret heart. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = internal:heart. The inner-being process: God's desire reaches into the deepest interior and seeks truthfulness there, and that desired honesty is coupled to a wisdom taught in the secret heart — truth as the moral condition of the hidden self, with God as the arena that both wants it and supplies its companion, wisdom.
narratives.story: In the middle of his confession, David realises what God is really after: not outward ceremony but honesty deep down, truth in the hidden, innermost self. This is the one place in these psalms where such truth is pictured as living in a specific inner room of a person — the secret heart rather than out in public. It is described as something God delights in and longs to find there, a settled condition of the self rather than an action the self performs. And it comes paired with wisdom: the same secret place where God wants truthfulness is where he teaches wisdom. So the picture is of God reaching into a person's most hidden depths, wanting real honesty there, and meeting that honesty with wisdom he himself imparts.
narratives.variation_note: This reading turns truth INWARD against Psa 45:4's outward cause. Only here is a seat recorded ('in the inward being') and the locus is internal:heart, with the bearer the penitent rather than the king; source and coupling are both present (what God desires / paired with wisdom in the secret heart). The move from a public championed truth to the honesty of the hidden self, and from 'no seat' to a located seat, is the finding: emeth ranges from banner to buried integrity.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = godly / faithful (chasid), read 'in the presence of the godly'. Type (102) is status — a standing identity, here that of a community. No source (103 present:false): the psalm does not derive this godly company from a stated cause; it is simply the fellowship the psalmist inhabits. Seat (104) = none — no organ locates it; belonging is not an organ-movement. Bearer (105) = the godly, the psalmist's company. Operation (106) = none and target (107) = none — the godly perform no discrete interior act here; the silence says their function is to BE the setting, the trustworthy fellowship in whose midst the psalmist acts. Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier, effect absent (109-111 present:false). Coupling (112) is a pair: the godly are the community in whose presence he waits and gives thanks — the item is bound to his acts of waiting and thanksgiving. No prohibition (113). Discovery (114): the faithful community, the psalmist's true company — the covenant-loyal among whom he waits and gives thanks, the opposite fellowship to the tyrant, a belonging that steadies hope. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = external:person. The inner-being process: over against the boastful, deceit-loving tyrant of vv1-4, the psalmist locates himself among the godly, and that belonging is what steadies his waiting and thanks — faithfulness here is a communal arena, other people, that holds and confirms the self's hope.
narratives.story: After denouncing a violent, boastful man who trusted in his riches, the psalmist places himself in very different company: he waits and gives thanks in the presence of the godly. These faithful people are not shown doing anything in particular; their role is simply to be the good and trustworthy circle he belongs to. Being among them is set right alongside his waiting on God and his thankfulness — this fellowship is the setting in which those acts happen. It is the exact opposite of the treacherous man he condemned. Belonging to this faithful community is what steadies him and confirms his hope; his own faith is held up by the trustworthy people around him.
narratives.variation_note: Here 'godly' is an external COMMUNITY (locus external:person; bearer the psalmist's company; coupled with his waiting and thanks) — belonging that steadies hope. It differs from Psa 12:1, where the godly are grieved as VANISHED (affect, internal loss), and from Psa 86:2, where the psalmist claims godliness as HIS OWN devotion (internal:ib-state, bearer the psalmist). The shift from lost-company to present-company to self-claim is the finding.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = be faithful (aman), negated — the item appears in its failure: a spirit that was NOT faithful. Type (102) is disposition: not a single act but a settled bent of the inner self, here a bent away from fidelity. No source (103 present:false): the psalm does not name a cause behind the unfaithfulness; it is presented as the generation's own condition. Seat (104) = none — no organ is named, though the verse speaks of heart and spirit generally; the reading declines to lodge the failure in a single faculty. Bearer (105) = the fathers, the stubborn and rebellious generation. Operation (106) = fail to be faithful — the interior movement is a non-movement, a withholding of fidelity. Target (107) = to God: the failed faithfulness is directed (negatively) toward God. Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier, effect absent (109-111 present:false) — no degree or downstream result is graded here, though the surrounding psalm supplies consequences; at the item itself the failure is simply stated. Coupling (112) = paired with the unsteady heart — the unfaithful spirit is welded to a heart that was not steadfast (v8). No prohibition (113). Discovery (114): 'whose spirit was not faithful to God' — the fidelity of heart the fathers lacked toward God. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = external:god — God is the one toward whom fidelity was owed and withheld. The inner-being process (directive 5, descent read fully): a whole generation's settled disposition is a heart that will not hold firm and a spirit that will not stay loyal — faithlessness as an ingrained bent, coupled to inner instability, aimed away from the God it should have trusted.
narratives.story: The psalm looks back at an earlier generation and describes them as stubborn and rebellious, with a spirit that would not stay loyal to God. This is not one bad moment but a settled inward tendency — a heart that refused to hold steady and a loyalty that kept slipping. The passage does not explain what made them this way; it simply names them as a people bent away from faithfulness. Their failure to stay true is aimed squarely at God, the one they owed loyalty to, and it is tied to a heart that was never firm in the first place. The picture is of unfaithfulness as a deep-seated trait: an unsteady inner core that would not commit itself to the God who had done wonders for them.
narratives.variation_note: This 'faithful' reading is a NEGATED failure of the fathers (disposition; operation 'fail to be faithful'; target to God; coupled with the unsteady heart) — the descent pole. Psa 78:37 repeats the failure but aims it 'to his covenant'; Psa 101:6 flips the item to ascent, the faithful in the land honoured with nearness (status). The variation is target (God / covenant) and valence (failure vs reward).

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = believe (aman), negated — belief in its absence: they did not believe. Type (102) is disposition, a settled inner bent (here toward distrust), not a passing thought. No source (103 present:false): no cause is named behind the unbelief; it is the people's own condition. Seat (104) = none — the psalm speaks of testing God 'in their heart' (v18) but the item is not lodged in a named organ; the failure is a whole-self posture. Bearer (105) = 'they', the wilderness generation. Operation (106) = fail to believe — the interior act is a refusal of trust. Target (107) = in God: the unbelief is aimed at God himself, not merely at circumstances. Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier, effect absent (109-111 present:false) — the degree and result are not graded at the item, though the psalm records God's wrath as consequence (v21). Coupling (112) = paired with not trusting his saving power — unbelief welded to a parallel failure of trust; the two negations reinforce each other. No prohibition (113). Discovery (114): 'because they did not believe in God' — the root unbelief beneath the complaint. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = external:god. The inner-being process: beneath the surface grumbling for food lies a settled interior refusal to trust God — unbelief as the root disposition, coupled with distrust of his saving power, and directed at God himself. Read as descent (directive 5), this shows faith's family in its cardinal failure: the interior will not rest its weight on God even after the rock gave water.
narratives.story: The people in the wilderness grumbled and doubted, demanding food and questioning whether God could really provide. The passage names the root under all that complaining: they did not believe in God and did not trust his power to save. This was not a one-off doubt but a settled inward refusal to lean on God. Their disbelief was aimed straight at God himself, not just at their hungry circumstances, and it went hand in hand with a refusal to trust that he could rescue them. Even after seeing water gush from a rock, they would not put their weight on him. The heart of their failure was this deep unwillingness to trust the God who kept proving himself.
narratives.variation_note: A NEGATED belief (disposition; 'fail to believe'; target 'in God'; coupled with not trusting his saving power) — belief as root unbelief. It differs from Psa 78:32 (also negated, but targeted at 'his wonders' and coupled with persistent sinning) and stands opposite the held/positive believing of Psa 27:13, 106:12, 116:10, 119:66. The variation across #2 and #3 is the object of unbelief: God himself vs his wonders.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = believe (aman), negated — again belief as failure: they did not believe. Type (102) is disposition, a fixed inner bent. No source (103 present:false): no cause is named; the unbelief simply persists. Seat (104) = none — not organ-located. Bearer (105) = 'they', the same generation. Operation (106) = fail to believe. Target (107) = in his wonders — and this is the distinctive: the unbelief here is aimed not merely at God's person but at his wonders, the very miracles they had witnessed. Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier, effect absent (109-111 present:false). Coupling (112) = paired with the persistent sinning — 'in spite of all this they still sinned'; unbelief welded to relentless, unrepentant sin. No prohibition (113). Discovery (114): 'and did not believe in his wonders' — unbelief that even miracles could not cure. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = external:god. The inner-being process, read at full weight (directives 5-6): the striking, uncomfortable finding is that miracles do not compel faith — the interior can witness wonders and still refuse to believe, the refusal now bound to continued sinning. This is a deeper stratum of unbelief than 78:22: not distrust before evidence, but distrust that survives overwhelming evidence, an inner hardness that miracles cannot dissolve.
narratives.story: Even after God gave the people everything they craved, and even after all his miracles, they kept right on sinning and still would not believe. This is unbelief at its most stubborn: not doubt for lack of proof, but doubt that no amount of proof could cure. They had seen his wonders with their own eyes, and their disbelief was aimed precisely at those wonders — as if the miracles counted for nothing. And it was locked together with ongoing, unrepentant sin. The uncomfortable truth the passage exposes is that seeing amazing things does not automatically create faith; a heart can witness the miraculous and remain hard, refusing to trust.
narratives.variation_note: Distinct from Psa 78:22 in its target and coupling: here unbelief is aimed at 'his wonders' (miracles already seen) and coupled with 'persistent sinning', whereas 78:22 aims at God directly and couples with distrust of his saving power. The finding of #3 is the deeper hardness — unbelief that even miracles cannot cure — as against the more general distrust of #2.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = be faithful (aman), negated — fidelity in its failure: they were not faithful. Type (102) is disposition, a settled bent. No source (103 present:false): no cause named. Seat (104) = none — though v37 names 'heart', the item is not lodged in a single organ. Bearer (105) = 'they', the generation whose mouths flattered while their hearts withheld. Operation (106) = fail to be faithful. Target (107) = to his covenant — the failed fidelity is owed specifically to the covenant, a bond of agreement, not merely to God's person in the abstract. Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier, effect absent (109-111 present:false). Coupling (112) = paired with the unsteady heart — 'their heart was not steadfast toward him' (v37); the covenant-unfaithfulness is welded to inner instability, exactly as at 78:8. No prohibition (113). Discovery (114): 'they were not faithful to his covenant' — the fidelity their words feigned but their hearts withheld. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = external:god. The inner-being process: the psalm exposes a split self — mouths that flatter and lie (v36) over a heart that will not hold firm; faithfulness fails not for lack of profession but for lack of an interior anchor. Faithlessness here is covenant-directed and heart-deep, the outward word contradicted by the inward instability it masks.
narratives.story: The people said the right things — they even flattered God with their mouths — but inside, their hearts were not steady and their loyalty did not hold. They were not faithful to the covenant, the solemn agreement they had made with God. The passage draws a sharp line between what they said and what they were: their words claimed devotion, but their inner selves never anchored to it. This broken loyalty was owed specifically to the covenant bond, and it grew straight out of a heart that refused to stay firm. The picture is of a divided person — smooth on the surface, unstable underneath — whose faithlessness was rooted in the very core that should have kept them true.
narratives.variation_note: The second failure-reading of 'faithful': like Psa 78:8 it is negated, disposition, coupled with the unsteady heart, but its target is 'to his covenant' rather than 'to God' — sharpening the failure as a breach of a specific bond, and set against a mouth that flatters (v36). Psa 101:6 remains the ascent counter-case (the faithful honoured). Variation = target and the word/heart split.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = faithful / godly ones (chasid). Type (102) is status — a standing identity, the covenant-faithful. No source (103 present:false): the psalm does not derive their faithfulness from a stated cause; they simply ARE God's devoted. Seat (104) = none — not organ-located. Bearer (105) = the godly ones (chasidim) of the people. Operation (106) = be the faithful, now slain — the item's movement is arrested: their only 'act' is to be God's faithful who have been killed. Target (107) = given to the beasts — the endpoint is their corpses handed to the beasts of the earth. Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier, effect absent (109-111 present:false). Coupling (112) = paired with the shame of the ravaged city — their outrage is welded to the defilement of temple and the ruin of Jerusalem. No prohibition (113). Discovery (114): 'the flesh of your faithful to the beasts of the earth' — the covenant-faithful, now corpses; their very faithfulness makes the outrage sharper — it is God's devoted who lie unburied. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = internal:ib-state. The inner-being process, read without comfort (directive 6): faithfulness here brings no protection — the godly are precisely the ones slaughtered and left for scavengers. The characteristic is filed as an inner-being state, yet its 'operation' is passive and terminal: to be faithful and dead. The finding is the scandal that devotion did not shield them; their identity as God's faithful only deepens the horror of their unburied bodies.
narratives.story: The nation has been overrun: the temple defiled, Jerusalem in ruins, and the bodies of God's faithful people left out as food for wild birds and beasts. The ones described here are the godly, those devoted to God — and that is exactly what makes the scene so shocking. Their faithfulness did not protect them; it is God's own loyal people who lie dead and unburied. Their devotion is not shown as anything they are doing now; their only condition is to be faithful and slain. The passage refuses any easy comfort: it faces head-on the fact that being true to God gave these people no shield, and that their very faithfulness makes the outrage against them all the more bitter.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = saints / godly (chasid). Type (102) is status — a standing identity, God's covenant-faithful. No source (103 present:false): their identity is not traced to a stated cause. Seat (104) = none — not organ-located. Bearer (105) = his saints. Operation (106) = be God's faithful. Target (107) = who hear his peace — the saints are defined by their receptivity, those to whom God speaks peace and who hear it. Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier, effect absent (109-111 present:false). Coupling (112) = paired with not turning to folly — 'but let them not turn back to folly' (v8); their standing as those who hear peace is welded to a warning against relapse. No prohibition (113 present:false) as a formal item, yet the coupling carries an implied 'let them not' — the reading files the not-turning as coupling rather than a prohibition proper, which is itself a distinction worth noting. Discovery (114): 'he will speak peace to his people, to his saints' — the covenant-faithful to whom God speaks peace, the godly community. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = internal:ib-state. The inner-being process: the saints are a listening people — their faithfulness shows as an interior receptivity that hears God's word of peace, held under the caution not to slide back into folly. Faith here is a posture of attentive hearing, poised between peace received and folly resisted.
narratives.story: The psalmist waits to hear what God will say, confident that God will speak peace to his own faithful people. These faithful ones are marked out by their listening — they are the people to whom God speaks peace and who actually hear it. But the promise comes with a caution attached: let them not slip back into foolishness. So their faithfulness is pictured as an attentive, receptive posture, an inner readiness to catch God's word of peace, held steady against the pull to relapse. They are a people defined not by loud activity but by quietly hearing their God, poised between the peace they receive and the folly they must keep resisting.
narratives.variation_note: Of the five 'saints' readings, this defines the godly by RECEPTIVITY — those who hear God's peace, coupled with a warning not to turn to folly (operation 'be God's faithful'; target 'who hear his peace'). It differs from Psa 97:10 (saints as those preserved/delivered from the wicked), Psa 116:15 (saints whose death is precious), and Psa 132:9/16 (saints who shout for joy). The operation is the axis of variation: hearing vs being preserved vs dying vs rejoicing.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = godly (chasid). Type (102) is status — a standing identity the psalmist claims for himself. No source (103 present:false): the godliness is not traced to a cause; it is asserted as his condition. Seat (104) = none — not organ-located. Bearer (105) = the psalmist — uniquely, here the speaker applies the term to HIMSELF ('preserve my life, for I am godly'). Operation (106) = be godly / devoted. Target (107) = to God — his devotion is directed Godward. Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier, effect absent (109-111 present:false). Coupling (112) = paired with trusting God — 'save your servant, who trusts in you'; godliness is welded to trust, the two named together. No prohibition (113). Discovery (114): 'preserve my life, for I am godly' — the covenant-devotion David claims, not merit but belonging to God. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = internal:ib-state. The inner-being process: the psalmist grounds his plea for preservation on his own godliness — but the reading is careful (directive 7) that this is not a boast of merit; it is a claim of belonging, of covenant-devotion, immediately coupled to trust in God. Faithfulness here is a self-understanding pressed into prayer: 'I belong to you, I trust you, therefore keep me' — the interior offering its own devotion as the ground of appeal.
narratives.story: David prays, 'Keep me alive, for I am one of your devoted ones,' and in the same breath calls himself the servant who trusts in God. He is claiming to be godly — but not bragging about how good he is. It is a claim of belonging: he is saying he is God's own, bound to him in loyalty, and that is why he asks to be kept safe. His devotion is aimed at God and comes tied together with trust in him. Here faithfulness becomes a kind of prayer: the psalmist offers his own loyalty and trust as the very reason God should preserve him, resting his appeal on the fact that he belongs to the God he is asking for help.
narratives.variation_note: The only 'godly' reading where the psalmist claims the trait for HIMSELF (bearer = the psalmist; operation 'be godly/devoted'; target to God; coupled with trusting God) — devotion pressed into a plea. It differs from Psa 12:1 (the godly grieved as vanished) and Psa 52:9 (the godly as an external community). Variation = bearer: self-claim vs lost others vs present company.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = saints (chasid). Type (102) is status — the godly, God's faithful. No source (103 present:false): their identity is not traced to a stated cause. Seat (104) = none — not organ-located. Bearer (105) = the saints, the godly. Operation (106) = be godly — a standing condition rather than a discrete act. Target (107) = preserved by God — the endpoint is their preservation: 'he preserves the lives of his saints.' Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier, effect absent (109-111 present:false). Coupling (112) is recorded as bound to the inner-being frame, and the locus item (116) carries the pairing with being delivered from the hand of the wicked — the two together weld the saints' standing to God's rescue of them out of the wicked's grasp (v10). No prohibition (113). Discovery (114): 'he preserves the lives of his saints' — the faithful whom God guards, the godly community. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = an inner-being state, paired with deliverance from the wicked. The inner-being process: the saints are defined here by being kept — their faithfulness (introduced by 'you who love the Lord, hate evil') is met by divine preservation and rescue from wicked hands. The interior movement implied is love-of-God-that-hates-evil, and the item's frame is the protected state of those God guards. Faith here is a guarded condition: to be God's saint is to be preserved and delivered.
narratives.story: Those who love the Lord are told to hate evil, and then comes the assurance: God guards the lives of his faithful ones and rescues them from the grip of the wicked. The saints here are defined by being kept safe — their faithfulness is answered by God's protection. Their inner devotion shows as a love for God that recoils from evil, and their standing is that of people held in God's care, snatched out of harm's way. To be one of these faithful is, in this passage, to be a protected person: someone whose loyalty to God is matched by God's steady guarding of their life against those who would destroy them.
narratives.variation_note: This 'saints' reading defines the godly by being PRESERVED and delivered from the wicked (operation 'be godly'; target 'preserved by God'; bound to deliverance from the wicked), and pairs with the call to love God and hate evil. It contrasts with Psa 85:8 (saints who hear peace), Psa 116:15 (saints whose death is precious), and Psa 132:9/16 (saints who shout for joy). Variation = the operation/outcome: guarded life vs hearing vs dying vs rejoicing.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = faithful (aman) — here in its positive form, the trustworthy. Type (102) is status — a standing quality, the faithful of the land. No source (103 present:false): their faithfulness is not traced to a cause; it is simply their character. Seat (104) = none — not organ-located. Bearer (105) = the faithful in the land. Operation (106) = be faithful. Target (107) = to God — their fidelity is Godward. Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier, effect absent (109-111 present:false). Coupling (112) is bound to the inner-being frame, and the locus item (116) carries the pairing with the blameless who minister — the faithful are welded to those who walk in the blameless way and so minister to the king (v6). No prohibition (113 as a formal item), though the psalm is thick with the king's refusals (he will not endure the arrogant, the deceitful shall not dwell with him) — the reading files the faithful positively, as those admitted rather than excluded. Discovery (114): 'I will look with favour on the faithful in the land' — the trustworthy whom the king honours, faithfulness rewarded with nearness. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = an inner-being state, paired with the blameless who minister. The inner-being process: in a psalm sorting the interior of a court — perverse hearts far off, arrogant looks not endured — the faithful are the ones drawn near; their fidelity to God is rewarded with dwelling-with and ministering-to the king. Faithfulness here is a trait that earns nearness, the positive counterpart to the deceit that is expelled.
narratives.story: The king sets out the kind of people he wants around him. He will not put up with the arrogant, the slanderer, or the liar — those are kept out of his house. But the faithful, the genuinely trustworthy people in the land, he looks on with favour and invites to live close to him and serve him. Their faithfulness is loyalty toward God, and it is rewarded with nearness: the trustworthy get to dwell with the king, while the deceitful are shut out. In a psalm all about who is welcomed and who is refused, faithfulness is the quality that draws a person in — the exact opposite of the dishonesty that gets someone expelled.
narratives.variation_note: The only ASCENT reading of 'faithful': the trustworthy are honoured with nearness (status; operation 'be faithful'; target to God; paired with the blameless who minister), the positive foil to the deceit the king expels. It reverses Psa 78:8 and 78:37, where 'faithful' appears negated as the fathers' covenant-failure. Variation = valence: reward vs failure.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = believe (aman) — belief in its positive form, but momentary. Type (102) is disposition. No source (103 present:false): the belief is not traced to a cause beyond the deliverance just witnessed. Seat (104) = none — not organ-located. Bearer (105) = the fathers. Operation (106) = believe. Target (107) = God's words — they believed his words after the sea covered their enemies. Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier, effect absent (109-111 present:false) — and the absence of any 'effect' item is telling against the narrative frame, since the psalm immediately records that 'they soon forgot' (v13); the item captures the belief without its collapse, which the passage supplies. Coupling (112)/locus (116): the belief is bound Godward and paired with singing his praise — belief welded to worship, 'then they believed his words; they sang his praise.' No prohibition (113). Discovery (114): 'then they believed his words' — the flash of faith after the sea's deliverance, belief that would not last. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = an act toward God, paired with singing praise. The inner-being process, read honestly (directive 6): here is belief that IS real and yet does not endure — faith kindled by rescue, expressed in praise, and then quickly forgotten. The finding is the fragility of gratitude-born faith: an interior that believes and sings in the moment of deliverance but has no staying power, sliding within verses into craving and testing.
narratives.story: The moment the sea closed over their enemies and God had saved them, the people believed his words and broke into song. It was genuine faith — real belief poured out in praise right after the rescue. But the passage does not let that stand as the whole story: almost at once, it adds, they forgot what God had done. So this is faith at its most fragile — a burst of trust and worship born from a dramatic deliverance, sincere in the moment but with no roots to hold it. Within a few lines they are back to craving and testing God. The picture is of belief that flares up in gratitude and then fades just as fast.
narratives.variation_note: A POSITIVE-but-fleeting believing (disposition; target 'God's words'; paired with singing praise), yet framed by the passage's 'they soon forgot'. It differs from the enduring belief of Psa 116:10 (held in affliction) and 119:66 (ground for a plea), and from the outright failures of Psa 78:22/32 and 106:24. Variation = durability: kindled-then-lost vs held-fast vs never-present.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = faith (aman), negated — faith in its absence: 'having no faith in his promise.' Type (102) is disposition, a settled inner bent, here toward distrust. No source (103 present:false): no cause named for the faithlessness. Seat (104) = none — not organ-located. Bearer (105) = the fathers. Operation (106) = have no faith. Target (107) = in God's promise — the unbelief is aimed specifically at God's promise (of the pleasant land). Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier, effect absent (109-111 present:false). Coupling (112)/locus (116): the faithlessness is bound Godward and paired with despising the land — 'they despised the pleasant land, having no faith in his promise'; unbelief welded to contempt for the very gift promised. No prohibition (113). Discovery (114): 'having no faith in his promise' — the unbelief that could not trust God to give the land. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = a failure toward God, paired with despising the land. The inner-being process, read at full weight: the interior refuses to trust God's promise and in the same movement despises the good he promised — faithlessness and contempt fused. The finding is that unbelief is not neutral hesitation but active scorn: to disbelieve the promise is to despise the pleasant land. Faith's failure here corrodes desire itself, so that the promised good becomes contemptible to the distrusting heart.
narratives.story: God had promised his people a good and pleasant land, but they would not trust him to give it. And their disbelief was not a mild uncertainty — in the same breath they despised the very land he had promised. Their refusal to have faith and their contempt for God's gift were fused together: not trusting the promise meant sneering at what was promised. The passage shows that unbelief is far from harmless neutrality; it actively poisons a person's desires, turning even a wonderful gift into something to be scorned. Their failure to trust God ruined their appetite for the good he was holding out to them.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = believe (aman) — belief in its positive, enduring form. Type (102) is disposition. No source (103 present:false): the belief is not derived from a stated cause; it is the speaker's own settled stance. Seat (104) = none — not organ-located. Bearer (105) = the psalmist. Operation (106) = believe. Target (107) = even in affliction — the belief holds precisely under distress: 'I believed, even when I spoke: I am greatly afflicted.' Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier, effect absent (109-111 present:false). Coupling (112)/locus (116): the believing is bound Godward and paired with being greatly afflicted — faith welded not to comfort but to suffering, believing THROUGH the affliction. No prohibition (113). Discovery (114): 'I believed, even when I spoke: I am greatly afflicted' — the faith that held even under affliction, belief speaking through pain. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = an act toward God, paired with affliction. The inner-being process: after being encircled by the snares of death and brought low, the psalmist testifies that he kept believing even as he confessed his suffering — belief that does not wait for relief but speaks in the midst of pain. The finding is faith's tenacity: an interior that holds its trust while openly naming its distress ('all mankind are liars', v11), belief and lament coexisting in the same breath.
narratives.story: The psalmist had been surrounded by the terrors of death and brought terribly low. Yet he testifies that even while he was crying out how badly he was suffering, he went on believing. His faith did not wait for the pain to lift — it spoke right in the middle of the anguish. This is trust at its toughest: not a confidence that only shows up once things are comfortable, but one that holds firm while a person is openly admitting how afflicted and even how disillusioned he feels. Belief and honest complaint live side by side here in the same breath. What the passage reveals is a faith that clings on through suffering rather than around it.
narratives.variation_note: Belief HELD under suffering (disposition; bearer the psalmist; target 'even in affliction'; paired with being greatly afflicted) — faith speaking through pain. It differs from the fleeting belief of Psa 106:12 (lost after rescue) and the plea-grounding belief of Psa 119:66, and reverses the failures of Psa 78:22/32. Variation = the condition under which belief operates: sustained amid affliction.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = saints (chasid). Type (102) is status — the godly, God's faithful. No source (103 present:false): not traced to a cause. Seat (104) = none — not organ-located. Bearer (105) = the saints. Operation (106) = be precious to God — the item's movement is not something the saints do but something they are TO God: precious. Target (107) = in their death — and this is the arresting turn: it is precisely their death that is precious in God's sight. Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier, effect absent (109-111 present:false). Coupling (112)/locus (116): the saints are bound to the inner-being frame and paired with the preciousness of their death. No prohibition (113). Discovery (114): 'Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints' — the godly, whose very death God holds dear. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = an inner-being state, paired with the preciousness of their death. The inner-being process, read without flinching (directive 6): the reading files this among the faithful characteristics, yet its content is that the saints' worth is measured at the point of death — God holds the dying of his faithful as costly, not cheap. The finding, set beside Psa 79:2 (the faithful slain and unburied), is the counterweight: there, faithfulness gave no earthly protection; here, the death of the faithful is not disregarded by God but held precious. The interior note is one of security-in-mortality — the saint's standing before God is not cancelled by death but honoured in it.
narratives.story: In the middle of giving thanks for being rescued from death, the psalmist makes a striking statement: the death of God's faithful people is precious in his sight. Their worth is weighed even at the moment of dying — God does not treat the passing of his devoted ones as cheap or unnoticed; he holds it dear. This sits as a quiet answer to the earlier horror of faithful people slaughtered and left unburied. There, their loyalty gave them no earthly protection; here, we learn that God still counts their deaths as costly to him. For the faithful, this offers a deep reassurance: their standing with God is not erased by death but honoured in it.
narratives.variation_note: The one 'saints' reading whose operation is to 'be precious to God' — and precious specifically 'in their death'. It contrasts sharply with Psa 85:8 (hearing peace), Psa 97:10 (preserved from the wicked), and Psa 132:9/16 (shouting for joy), and answers Psa 79:2 (faithful slain, unprotected) with the counter-note that their death is held dear. Variation = the operation is death-valued, not action or rescue.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = believe (aman) — belief in its positive form. Type (102) is disposition, a settled stance. No source (103 present:false): not derived from a stated cause. Seat (104) = none — not organ-located. Bearer (105) = the psalmist. Operation (106) = believe. Target (107) = God's word — specifically 'I believe in your commandments.' Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier, effect absent (109-111 present:false). Coupling (112) = paired within its char-arc across the psalm — belief is welded not to one adjacent phrase but to the whole psalm's sustained devotion to God's word (keeping precepts, delighting in the law, hoping in the word). No prohibition (113). Discovery (114): 'Teach me good judgment and knowledge, for I believe in your commandments' — faith in the commandments as the ground for the plea to be taught. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = external:god. The inner-being process: belief here functions as the GROUND of a request — the psalmist asks to be taught good judgment and knowledge precisely because he already believes God's commandments. Faith is not the endpoint but the foundation from which he reaches for more understanding; it authorises the plea. The finding is belief as productive trust: an interior conviction in God's word that generates hunger to learn it better, faith motivating instruction rather than resting content.
narratives.story: The psalmist prays to be taught good judgment and knowledge, and he gives his reason: he already believes in God's commandments. His faith is not the finish line but the starting point — because he trusts God's word, he wants to understand it better and asks to be taught. Throughout this long psalm that same believing runs like a thread: he keeps God's instructions, delights in his law, and hopes in his word. What stands out here is that faith actually drives him to learn more; his conviction that God's commands are true makes him hungry to grasp them more deeply. Belief becomes the engine of his desire for understanding, not a place to sit still.
narratives.variation_note: Belief as the GROUND of a plea to be taught (disposition; bearer the psalmist; target 'God's word/commandments'; coupled across the whole psalm's arc) — faith that generates hunger to learn. It differs from Psa 27:13 (belief as felt anchor), Psa 106:12 (fleeting), and Psa 116:10 (held in affliction). Variation = function: belief authorising a request for instruction.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = faithless (bagad) — treachery, the active betrayer. This is the family's Sin-cluster item, and it is read at full weight (directive 5). Type (102) is status — a standing identity, the treacherous. No source (103 present:false): no cause is named for their treachery. Seat (104) = none — not organ-located. Bearer (105) = the faithless. Operation (106) = deal faithlessly — an active betrayal, not a mere lack. Target (107) = the psalmist — their treachery is aimed at him ('many are my persecutors and my adversaries'). Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier, effect absent (109-111 present:false). Coupling (112) = paired within its char-arc across the psalm — the faithless are set against the whole psalm's devotion, the dark foil to the speaker's love of God's law. No prohibition (113). Discovery (114): 'I look at the faithless with disgust, because they do not keep your commands' — the treacherous who spurn God's commands. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = external:person — these are other people, the arena against which the psalmist's own fidelity is defined. The inner-being process: the faithless are those who actively break faith and spurn God's commands, and the psalmist's response is disgust — an interior recoil. The finding is that faithlessness is here observed from OUTSIDE the self, as the trait of adversaries, and it provokes a felt revulsion in the observer; the item does double duty, naming both the betrayers' standing and the loathing they stir in the faithful heart. Faith and faithlessness are read as mutually defining: the psalmist knows his own loyalty partly by his disgust at their treachery.
narratives.story: The psalmist looks at the treacherous people around him — the ones who break faith and simply ignore God's commands — and he feels disgust. These are his persecutors and adversaries, and their betrayal is aimed at him. Their faithlessness is not merely a gap or a weakness; it is an active treachery, a deliberate spurning of what God has said. The passage names them from the outside, as other people whose disloyalty stands in stark contrast to the psalmist's own love for God's law. And it names his gut reaction: revulsion. In a way, his loathing of their treachery helps him know his own loyalty — he sees clearly who he is by recoiling from who they are.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = saints (chasid). Type (102) is status — the godly, God's faithful. No source (103 present:false): not traced to a cause. Seat (104) = none — not organ-located. Bearer (105) = the saints. Operation (106) = shout for joy — an active, vocal jubilation. Target (107) = before God — the shout is directed into God's presence, in the setting of the ark coming to its resting place. Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier, effect absent (109-111 present:false) — notably no intensity is graded even though 'shout for joy' is intrinsically loud; the silence declines to measure the joy's degree. Coupling (112)/locus (116): the saints are bound to the inner-being frame and paired with the shout of joy itself — the item is welded to its own expression. No prohibition (113). Discovery (114): 'and let your saints shout for joy' — the godly, whose response to God's presence is jubilant. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = an inner-being state, paired with the shout of joy. The inner-being process: here the faithful are defined by an OUTWARD, exuberant response — a joy that erupts into a shout as the ark (God's presence) is brought to its rest, set parallel to the priests being clothed with righteousness (v9). The finding is that faithfulness in this reading is not quiet receptivity or endurance but jubilation: the interior of the godly overflows into vocal joy in God's presence.
narratives.story: As the ark of God is brought to its resting place, the psalm calls for the priests to be clothed with righteousness and for God's faithful people to shout for joy. Here the godly are defined by their exuberance: their response to God's presence bursts out as a loud, glad shout. This is not a quiet, inward faith but a joy that cannot stay contained — it erupts into celebration right there before God. Their faithfulness shows itself in jubilation, an overflow of gladness at having God near. Where other passages picture the faithful listening, or being kept safe, or facing death, this one paints them simply rejoicing out loud in God's presence.
narratives.variation_note: A 'saints' reading defined by JUBILATION — shouting for joy 'before God' as the ark comes to rest. Nearly twinned with Psa 132:16, it differs by target: here the shout is 'before God' (in his presence), whereas 132:16 shouts 'at God's salvation'. Both contrast with the receptivity of Psa 85:8, the preservation of Psa 97:10, and the death-value of Psa 116:15. Variation = target/occasion of the same joyful operation.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = saints (chasid). Type (102) is status — the godly of Zion. No source (103 present:false): not traced to a cause. Seat (104) = none — not organ-located. Bearer (105) = the saints. Operation (106) = shout for joy — the same jubilant vocal act as at 132:9. Target (107) = at God's salvation — here the joy is aimed at the salvation God gives ('her priests I will clothe with salvation, and her saints will shout for joy'); the shout answers God's saving act. Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier, effect absent (109-111 present:false). Coupling (112)/locus (116): the saints are bound to the inner-being frame and paired with the shout of joy. No prohibition (113). Discovery (114): 'her saints will shout for joy' — the godly of Zion, jubilant at the salvation that clothes them. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = an inner-being state, paired with the shout of joy. The inner-being process: this reading places the same jubilation as a RESPONSE to divine salvation — God's promise to clothe the priests with salvation is met by the saints' shout. Where 132:9 was a petition ('let your saints shout') set before God's presence at the ark, 132:16 is God's own promise ('her saints WILL shout') answering his gift of salvation. The finding, in the difference (directive 10), is a shift from prayer to fulfilment: the same joyful faithfulness moves from something asked for in God's presence to something guaranteed in response to his saving act.
narratives.story: God himself makes a promise about Zion: he will clothe her priests with salvation, and her faithful people will shout for joy. The godly here are again marked by jubilation, but now that joy is a response to what God gives — they shout because of the salvation he pours out. And there is a subtle shift from the earlier scene: before, the shout was something prayed for as the ark came near; here it is something God guarantees will happen once he has saved his people. The same overflowing gladness moves from a request into a promised certainty. The faithful are pictured as a people whose natural answer to God's rescue is loud, unrestrained joy.
narratives.variation_note: Twin to Psa 132:9 in operation (shout for joy) but differing in target and mood: here the joy is 'at God's salvation' and framed as God's own PROMISE ('her saints WILL shout'), whereas 132:9 is a PETITION ('let your saints shout') before God's presence at the ark. The move from prayer to guaranteed fulfilment is the finding. Both differ from the non-jubilant saints of Psa 85:8, 97:10, 116:15.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = the honour of executing judgment — the item names not the deed as such but the DIGNITY felt in carrying out the decreed judgment. Type (102) is affect: this is a felt state, honour experienced, not the volitional act itself. No source (103 present:false): the honour is not traced to a stated cause. Seat (104) = none — not organ-located. Bearer (105) = the godly. Operation (106) = to carry out the written judgment is the honour of all God's saints — dignity in obedience. Target (107) = dignified-obedience: the endpoint is the sense of dignity in obeying. Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier, effect absent (109-111 present:false). Coupling (112) = honour-in-judgment — the felt honour welded to the act of judgment. No prohibition (113). Discovery (114): 'to execute on them the judgment written! This is honour for all his godly ones' — the operation is the sense of dignity in performing the decreed judgment; obedience felt as honour. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = internal:ib-state. The inner-being process, read without softening (directives 5-6): the godly experience carrying out God's written judgment — including vengeance and punishment on nations and kings (vv7-8) — as HONOUR, a dignity that fills the interior. This is faithfulness felt as elevation: the self esteems its own obedience as glory. The uncomfortable finding is that the interior here binds violence-as-obedience to a sense of dignity and glory ('let the godly exult in glory', v5); the faith-family surfaces an affect in which executing decreed judgment is felt as honourable, not troubling.
narratives.story: The psalm ends by declaring that to carry out God's written judgment is an honour for all his faithful people. The focus here is on a feeling: the sense of dignity and glory the godly experience in doing what God has decreed. Their obedience is not felt as a grim burden but as something that elevates them — a privilege that fills them with a sense of worth. Earlier the psalm has them exulting in glory and singing for joy, and now that same exalted mood attaches to executing judgment on the nations and their kings. The passage does not tidy this away: it plainly presents the faithful experiencing the carrying out of God's judgment, violence included, as an honour — obedience felt as glory rather than as something troubling.
narratives.variation_note: The two 'execute' readings split the same act into two inner registers. This one is the AFFECT: the FELT honour and dignity of carrying out the decreed judgment (sense 'the honour of executing judgment'; target dignified-obedience; coupling honour-in-judgment). Psa 149:7 is the VOLITION: the will/agency actually to execute the vengeance. Variation = type (affect vs volition) — the felt glory of obeying vs the resolve to act.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101) = execute the decreed vengeance — here the item names the ACT/agency of carrying out vengeance, not the feeling about it. Type (102) is volition: this is the will and agency, the interior resolve turned into commissioned action. No source (103 present:false): the resolve is not traced to a stated cause within the self — importantly, the judgment is 'not self-devised' (see discovery), so its origin lies in God's decree, not the agent's own impulse; the reading leaves the interior source unrecorded. Seat (104) = none — not organ-located. Bearer (105) = the godly. Operation (106) = the godly are agents to execute vengeance on the nations and punishments on the peoples. Target (107) = agency-of-judgment: the endpoint is the godly acting as commissioned agents. Manner (108) = none; intensity, specifier, effect absent (109-111 present:false). Coupling (112) = execute-vengeance — the volition welded to the vengeance-act. No prohibition (113). Discovery (114): 'to execute vengeance on the nations and punishments on the peoples' — the interior resolve turns outward as commissioned action, carrying out a judgment not self-devised. Role (115) = characteristic; locus (116) = internal:ib-state. The inner-being process, read at full weight: the godly hold high praises of God in their throats and two-edged swords in their hands (v6), and the interior movement is a resolve to act as agents of a judgment God has already decreed. The finding, distinguished from 149:9 (directive 8), is that here the item is the WILL to carry out — an agency, a settled resolve to execute — rather than the honour felt in it. Faithfulness surfaces as a militant volition: the interior aligns its will to God's decree and turns outward into action, with the crucial qualification that the judgment is received, not invented by the self.
narratives.story: With praises of God in their mouths and swords in their hands, the faithful set themselves to carry out vengeance on the nations and punishment on the peoples. The focus here is on the will to act — the settled resolve to do it, the interior turning outward into real action. This is not the feeling about the task but the readiness to perform it, the godly stepping up as agents. One thing matters a great deal: the judgment they carry out is not one they dreamed up themselves; it is a verdict God has already decreed, and they are executing it on his behalf. So the passage shows the faithful bending their will to God's decision and moving to act on it — a resolve to carry out a judgment they received rather than invented.
narratives.variation_note: The VOLITION half of the 'execute' pair: the will/agency to carry out the decreed vengeance (type volition; operation 'the godly are agents to execute vengeance'; coupling execute-vengeance), with the qualification that the judgment is 'not self-devised'. Psa 149:9 is the AFFECT half — the felt honour of the same obedience. Variation = type (volition vs affect): the resolve to act vs the dignity felt in acting.
